title: Seven Days in the Saddle
statement: A cyclist rides on each of $7$ consecutive days. The mean distance ridden per day is $10$ km over the first $4$ days, $16$ km over the last $4$ days, and $12$ km over all $7$ days. How many kilometres does the cyclist ride on the fourth day?
hints: Means are awkward to combine directly. For each of the three groups of days, work out the total distance ridden.

Each group's total is its mean multiplied by its number of days. Now use inclusion-exclusion: the first four days and the last four days together cover the whole week, so ask which day belongs to both groups.

The three totals are $40$ km for the first four days, $64$ km for the last four days and $84$ km for the week. Adding the first two totals counts day $4$ twice and every other day once, so this sum exceeds the week's total by exactly the distance ridden on day $4$.
solution: A mean is the total divided by the number of days, so each total is the mean multiplied by the number of days. The first $4$ days total $4 \cdot 10 = 40$ km, the last $4$ days total $4 \cdot 16 = 64$ km, and all $7$ days total $7 \cdot 12 = 84$ km. The first four days are days $1$ to $4$, and the last four days are days $4$ to $7$. Day $4$ is in both groups, and each other day is in exactly one. So the sum $40 + 64$ counts every day's distance once and then counts day $4$ a second time. In other words, $40 + 64$ equals the week's total plus the distance on day $4$. The distance on day $4$ is therefore $40 + 64 - 84 = 20$ km. The other six distances are not fixed individually, but this does not matter, as the argument never uses them. The cyclist rides $20$ km on the fourth day, so the answer is $20$. Why this works. inclusion-exclusion, linear-combination-of-equations: two overlapping groups cover the week and share only day $4$, so adding their totals and subtracting the week's total isolates that day.
